items.summary: A 26-year-old woman named Hema Vajjiparthi was killed after a state transport bus allegedly crashed into a two-wheeler. Panjagutta police booked the driver, Sheik Anwar, and reportedly arrested him on the same day. He was booked under sections 106(1) (causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide) and 125(a) (act endangering life of others) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and section 184 (driving dangerously) of the Motor Vehicles Act. Hema was a native of East Godavari district in Andhra Pradesh and was working as a customer relationship executive at a car showroom in Banjara Hills, according to reports . items.title: Urvashi’s Aasha is refreshing because its women are allowed to be complicated
items.summary: Cinema has rarely allowed women the complexity of being human. Female characters are most often expected to be virtuous, predictable, and ideal. Even when women are placed at the centre of the narrative, few and far as they are, the contradictions are neatly ironed out into palatable ideas of femininity. Aasha , however, offers an interesting aside. Directed by Safar Sanal, the Malayalam film released on September 11. “I have never lived for myself,” says Urvashi’s titular character, in a moment of absolute frenzy. That line forms the defining conscience of the film, which presents Aasha and her daughter Anagha (Aishwarya Lekshmi) as neither entirely condemnable nor fully likeable – a welcome departure from the restrictive iterations of women on the silver screen. The film opens at a bank. Aasha waits patiently for her turn, though visibly restless. Soon enough, we meet the short-tempered, stubborn woman beneath the one who puts up with everything, one who is not reluctant to make a scene at the slightest hint of disrespect.
